one_liner: 223-line CC0 header of single-threaded C++11 signals; beats Boost.Signals2 (st) and libsigc++ in a community MSVC shootout.
what_it_does: Simple::Signal<R(Args...), Collector> holds a list of callbacks; connect() takes anything convertible to std::function and returns a size_t connection ID, disconnect(id) removes it, and emit(args...) calls every handler in connection order. Collectors decide what emit() returns (last result by default, or a std::vector of all results, or stop at the first zero/non-zero result), and Simple::slot() binds an object to a member function. The interface differs from Boost.Signals2: no connection objects, scoped connections or lifetime tracking, so code written against Boost needs porting.
how_it_is_fast: Since a 2018 pull request (#4, leira) each signal is a plain std::list of std::shared_ptr<std::function>, and emit() is a range-for over that list with no locking, no connection bookkeeping and no reference counting per step; that PR reported 4.7 ns per emission versus 22.4 ns for Tim Janik's original ref-counted linked ring. There is no mutex, no slot-group ordering, no tracked-object checks and no combiner machinery, which is where Boost.Signals2 spends its time even in its dummy-mutex build. The signal object is 16 bytes on MSVC (a std::list).
when_to_use: Single-threaded event plumbing (UI, game loop, tool code) where a handful of handlers are connected once and emitted often, and Boost.Signals2's features are not needed.
Projects that want a vendorable public-domain (CC0) header with no dependencies beyond the standard library and only C++11.

Replacing Boost.Signals2 in its single-thread configuration or libsigc++ where profiling shows connect or emit overhead: the shootout shows 2.7x faster connect and 3.1x faster emit than Boost Signals2 st on MSVC.
Handlers that take arguments by reference or pointer (as the benchmark's Rng& does), so per-slot argument copies cost nothing.
when_not_to_use: Any handler that may disconnect itself or another handler while emit() is running: since the 2018 std::list rewrite this erases list nodes under the running range-for (use-after-free, skipped handlers), even though the header comment still promises it is safe.
Multi-threaded code: nothing is synchronised; connect, disconnect and emit from different threads race.

When you need the fastest lightweight signal: in the same shootout jeffomatic jl_signal (score 415,278), vdksoft signals st (309,575), Nuclex Events (215,607) and nano-signal-slot st (196,413) all score higher, and on the combined connect/emit/disconnect column SimpleSignal (4,619) ranks 17th of 24, about 5.4x behind jl_signal (24,950).
Code that needs automatic disconnection when the receiver dies, scoped connections, slot groups or blocking: none exist, and IDs must be stored and disconnected by hand.
Long-lived projects: the repo has had no commits since 2019-07-24, no issues ever filed and no test for recursion or disconnect-during-emit.

integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (test.cpp builds with g++ -std=gnu++11; the shootout built it with Visual Studio 2019 x64 under C++17)
integration.platforms: any platform with a C++11 standard library
integration.thread_safety: None: no locking anywhere; a signal must be used from one thread (the shootout lists it as not thread-safe and runs no threaded test for it).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same connect/disconnect/emit idea, but connect returns a size_t ID instead of a boost::signals2::connection, there are no scoped connections, tracking, groups or shared_connection_block, and the default return-value collector returns the last result rather than an optional.

gotchas: Disconnect during emission is undefined behaviour in the current code (and in the copy the shootout benchmarked): disconnect() runs std::remove_if plus erase on the std::list that emit() is iterating, and emit() holds only a reference to the current shared_ptr. If the last handler disconnects itself, its list node is freed and the loop then increments a dangling iterator; if an earlier handler disconnects itself, its std::function is destroyed while executing and the next handler is skipped for that emission. The original ref-counted ring (removed in PR #4, August 2018) deferred deletion and was safe; the header's 'safe against recursion, so callbacks may be removed ... during a signal emission' comment was not updated, and the leftover if (slot) check never fires.

Connection IDs are the heap address of the stored std::function (size_t(ptr.get())); after a disconnect the allocator can hand the same address to a later connect, so a stale ID can disconnect an unrelated newer handler.

Each connect costs two heap allocations (the std::list node and the make_shared block), plus any heap storage std::function needs for a large callable; disconnect is a linear scan of the whole list, so removing all N handlers is O(N^2).

Arguments are taken by value in emit() and again per handler in the internal invoke() and std::function call, so a by-value std::string parameter is copied several times per emission; use const references in the signature. Handlers connected during an emission are appended and called in that same emission.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The siblings (Delegate, stdext::inplace_function, SmallFunction, woid, sy_callback.hpp) replace a single std::function; SimpleSignal is a multicast list built on std::function, so pick it only when you need one-to-many callbacks with result collectors, and consider storing one of those faster delegates instead of std::function if you patch it. CDRC and observable_unique_ptr solve ownership, not callbacks.
verified_claims_summary: In NoAvailableAlias/signal-slot-benchmarks (MSVC, Visual Studio 2019 x64 release, flags, CPU and Boost version not stated), SimpleSignal's thread-unsafe-table averages over N = 2..64 handlers are emit 137,345 vs Boost Signals2 st 44,228 (3.1x) and libsigc++ 72,139 (1.9x), connect 9,994 vs 3,655 (2.7x), disconnect 9,745 vs 9,734 (tie), combined 4,619 vs 2,265 (2.0x) and 1,201 (3.8x), for a total score of 170,724 vs 62,979 and 80,450 (derived from page data). Harness caveat: each emit sample is one 2-64-handler emission between two high_resolution_clock::now() calls and the score truncates the mean to whole nanoseconds (size_t limit/count) before inverting, so the emit column, which makes up 80% of SimpleSignal's score, clusters at 130,000-137,345 for 14 of 24 thread-unsafe libraries and does not separate lightweight implementations.
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-07-24 (26 commits, no issues filed); CC0 public domain and small enough to vendor, but patch disconnect() (defer removal, for example by nulling the slot and compacting after emission) before relying on the header's recursion-safety promise.
